newsitem.title: USA: CDC says steps taken to improve nuclear security.
newsitem.headline: CDC says steps taken to improve nuclear security.

text.p: Federal health officials said Thursday they had taken corrective steps since a surprise inspection by federal regulators found possible violations of rules for the handling of nuclear materials at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
An unannounced inspection of the CDC by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) on May 27 found two instances in which nuclear materials were stored in unlocked containers in unlocked rooms.

"We are taking this extremely seriously," Jack Jackson, the CDC's associate director of management and operations, told an NRC panel. The CDC, a group of federal agencies that monitors infectious and preventable diseases, uses nuclear material in medical research.
"This is a serious concern for us. We are a national depository for infectious diseases," Jonathan Richmond, the CDC's director of occupational health and safety, said.
Richmond said more attention would be paid to locking doors and keeping nuclear material secure. He stressed that only CDC employees had access to laboratories where nuclear materials were stored.
"There have not been any adverse health or safety ramifications to employees or the community," he said.

The NRC said the CDC had not met its own guidelines for locking radioactive materials in refrigerators where they were being stored. "I don't think I saw a single lock on a refrigerator in the place," NRC inspector Orysia Masnyk Bailey said.

In a letter to the CDC, the NRC said it also found apparent violations of policies involving record-keeping, instrument accuracy and signs, which "seem to indicate a lack of management oversight and failure to adhere to license conditions."
The NRC said it would announce within the next month whether it had concluded that the violations occurred and whether sanctions were needed.

The apparent violations include the failure to secure licensed radioactive material from unauthorized use and removal; the failure to perform periodic inventories of licensed material; repeated failures to ensure that radiation survey meters were calibrated annually; and the failure to remove unnecessary signs from previously restricted areas, the NRC said.
